column2: The Rahimi Family
A made-up family
Mr Rahimi wants to put all the family’s savings into the stock market and take broker credit too. You need to sort the family’s money into buckets.
The family’s finances
Total savings: 900 million tomans
Living costs: 30 million tomans a month
Goal: a home down payment, 400 million tomans, 2 years from now
Mr Rahimi: “Let’s put it all into the market; we’ll take broker credit too so we get rich faster.”
1 month of costs
At least 6 months of costs
1 to 3-year goal
The whole goal amount
Whatever is left
With the minimum rule (6 months of costs), how many million tomans is the emergency fund?
6 × 30 = 180 million tomans, outside stocks.
After setting aside 1 month of current costs, a 6-month emergency fund and the home money, how much is left for stocks?
900 − 30 − 180 − 400 = 290 million tomans; only this money has a 5-year horizon.
Put each pot of the family’s money in its right place.
Fixed income or Akhza
30 million for this month’s costs
180 million emergency fund
400 million home down payment
290 million long-term
Current costs in a bank account; the emergency fund and the 2-year goal in fixed income or Akhza; only long-term money in stocks.
Where does the broker-credit proposal sit in the family’s investment statement?
On the “never” list; leverage is banned
Allowed, if the market is rising
Allowed, up to half the capital
Leverage, buying on signals and borrowed money are the statement’s three “nevers”.
Because stocks return more over the long run, it’s better to put the home money into the market too.
2-year money has a short horizon; a 40% fall within a year is possible and the home purchase would be delayed.
Explain to Mr Rahimi in 2 to 4 sentences why only 290 million tomans goes into stocks.

This month’s costs and the emergency fund must stay within reach so we aren’t forced to sell in a market fall. We need the home money in 2 years, and a short horizon doesn’t fit stock swings; it belongs in fixed income or Akhza. Only money we won’t need for 5 years or more, that is 290 million, goes into stocks.
Current costs and the emergency fund must stay outside stocks and within reach
The home money has a short horizon and shouldn’t be in stocks
Only long-term money (5 years and up) goes into stocks
Each pot of money goes where its horizon allows.
Mr Kazemi’s 40 Percent Gain
A made-up investor
Mr Kazemi tells everyone he made 40% last year. You need to work out whether he really got richer, and what kind of reason he bought for.
The claim and last year’s numbers
Mr Kazemi: “Last year my portfolio grew 40%. I saw a buy queue and retail money coming in, and I bought.”
Last year’s nominal return
Mr Kazemi’s stock portfolio
Gold coin
Yearly inflation
What is the real return of Mr Kazemi’s portfolio, in percent? (one decimal place)
1.40 ÷ 1.45 − 1 ≈ minus 3.4%; his purchasing power went down.
What is the real return of the fixed-income fund, in percent? (one decimal place)
Which asset kept its purchasing power last year?
1.50 ÷ 1.45 − 1 ≈ plus 3.4%; only the gold coin beat inflation.
What kind of reason is Mr Kazemi’s reason for buying (“a buy queue and retail money coming in”)?
Price behaviour and money flow, not the value of the business
Fundamental analysis with Codal reports and financial statements
Valuation on the company’s sustainable profit
Queues and retail money are trading-board data. In FIS, stocks are chosen with Codal and the Golden Three, and board data is only for timing.
A 40% nominal gain means Mr Kazemi’s wealth has grown.
With 45% inflation, his money buys less today than it did last year.
In 2 to 4 sentences, tell Mr Kazemi why his 40% wasn’t a real gain and what he should compare returns with next time.

His real return is about minus 3.4%, because 45% inflation was higher than his 40% return; so his purchasing power went down. Every return must be compared with inflation and with other options such as Akhza, fixed-income funds and gold coins. And the reason for buying should be the value of the business, not a buy queue.
45% inflation is higher than the 40% return; the real return is negative
It must be compared with inflation and other options (Akhza, gold coins, fixed income)
The reason for buying must be fundamental, not queues or money flow
Nominal fools you; always work out the real return.
Firuzeh Tile
A made-up company
Firuzeh Tile’s audited annual financial statements are out. You need to work out where the profit came from, how much turned into cash, and what the auditor said.
Annual income statement (billion rials)
1,000 million shares. Note 28: of the 600 billion of other income, 550 billion is a gain on selling the old factory’s land.
Amount
Operating income
Cash flow and the auditor’s report
Cash from operations (CFO): 1,530 billion rials
Auditor’s opinion: qualified. The qualification: the auditor wasn’t present at the year-end stock count and couldn’t confirm inventory of 900 billion rials.
What is the gross profit margin, in percent?
What is the operating profit margin, in percent?
Which item is one-off and doesn’t go into sustainable profit?
The gain on selling the old factory’s land
Selling and admin costs
Selling land doesn’t repeat; 550 billion of the 600 billion of other income is one-off.
What is the ratio of operating cash to net profit (CFO/NI)? (two decimal places)
1,530 ÷ 1,700 = 0.9; above 0.8, profit has turned into cash.
What does a “qualified” opinion about inventory mean?
An important but limited problem; estimate the qualification’s effect
The statements as a whole are misleading and the company is off the list
Everything was confirmed with no problems
Qualified opinions are common in Iran; what matters is the amount. 900 billion of inventory against 1,700 billion of profit isn’t small.
Sum up Firuzeh Tile in 2 to 4 sentences: does its main business make profit? Is its profit high quality? What should be followed up?

The main business makes profit: a gross margin of 30% and an operating margin of 20%. But 550 billion of the 1,700 billion net profit comes from selling land and won’t repeat. Profit turned into cash well (CFO/NI 0.9), but the auditor’s qualification about 900 billion of inventory must be followed up.
The main business makes profit (gross margin 30%, operating 20%)
Part of net profit is one-off (the land sale)
Profit turned into cash (CFO/NI 0.9), but the inventory qualification must be followed up
Three questions every time: from the main business? Turned into cash? What did the auditor say?
Shafagh Petrochemical
Shafagh Petrochemical’s autumn monthly reports show sales revenue growing, and then a fire announcement came out. You need to pull the numbers apart.
Sales volume (tonnes)
Price (million rials per tonne)
Mehr
Aban
Azar
Material information, 10 Dey
“Because of a fire in one of the units, about 20% of production capacity will be stopped from Dey to the end of Bahman (2 months). The equipment is insured.”
By how many percent did Azar’s sales revenue grow over Mehr’s?
By how many percent did Azar’s selling price grow over Mehr’s?
Where did the growth in sales revenue come from?
Only from price; sales volume fell 10%
From volume and price, both together
Only from volume; the price stayed the same
Volume went from 20,000 to 18,000 tonnes (minus 10%). Rising revenue with falling volume is a warning pattern.
If the stop removes 20% of Azar’s monthly sales revenue for 2 months, how many billion rials is the drop in sales?
9,000 × 20% × 2 = 3,600; about 3% of yearly sales, which at Azar’s price are about 108 thousand billion.
What does this announcement mean for sustainable profit?
Its effect is temporary; this year’s profit falls but sustainable profit doesn’t
It cuts sustainable profit by 20% for good because capacity is lost
It has no effect at all because there is insurance
A 2-month stop is temporary. How much the insurance covers will become clear in later announcements.
A capital increase from retained earnings brings new money into the company.
No new money comes in; it’s the same as not paying out profit, in favour of a project.
In 2 to 4 sentences, write what you’ll look for in Shafagh Petrochemical’s Dey and Bahman monthly reports, and why.

First sales and production volume: whether the fall in volume continues and how big the effect of the 20% stop is. Then the selling price: whether the price growth lasts. And whether capacity returns after 2 months and how much insurance covers, to know whether the effect is temporary.
Sales and production volume (whether the volume fall continues, and the stop’s effect)
The selling price and whether its growth lasts
Capacity returning after 2 months, or insurance cover (whether the effect is temporary)
Monthly reports are the best place to see whether an event is temporary or permanent.
Sina Mehr Pharma
Sina Mehr’s 6-month net profit grew 47% and the channels are excited. Read the report page line by line.
6-month interim income statement, unaudited (billion rials)
Note 25, other non-operating income: 400 billion rials of currency translation gains.
This year’s 6 months
Last year’s 6 months
Previous financial year (audited)
Balance sheet (billion rials)
End of the 6-month period
End of the previous financial year
Trade receivables
Which column do you compare this year’s 6-month profit with?
Previous financial year
Neither
Compare periods of the same length; don’t measure 6 months against 12.
By how many percent did 6-month net profit grow over last year’s 6 months? (one decimal place)
By how many percent did operating profit grow over the same period? (one decimal place)
960 ÷ 880 − 1 ≈ 9.1%; most of the net profit growth comes from the 400-billion translation gain.
What does “(80)” on the finance costs line mean?
A negative number; it is subtracted from profit
An 80 percent change on last year
An unaudited, provisional number
Brackets in financial statements mean negative.
By how many percent did trade receivables grow from the end of last year to the end of the period?
3,600 ÷ 2,400 − 1 = 50%, while 6-month sales grew 20%.
What does 50% receivables growth against 20% sales growth signal?
Credit sales have grown; profit quality needs checking
A sign of complete health and customer growth; more sales means more receivables
It has nothing to do with profit; it’s only the balance sheet
Profit was recorded but a bigger part of it hasn’t turned into money yet; look at the receivables and related-party notes.
In 2 to 4 sentences, explain why Sina Mehr’s 47% net profit growth isn’t as good as it looks.

Most of the growth is from a 400-billion currency translation gain, which is non-operating and probably one-off; operating profit grew only about 9%. Receivables also grew 50%, much faster than sales, so part of the profit hasn’t turned into cash yet.
Most of the growth is from a currency translation gain (non-operating, one-off)
Operating profit grew only about 9%
Receivables grew much faster than sales (profit quality)
Always ask which line the profit growth came from.
Kuhsar Cement
A channel wrote: “Kuhsar Cement’s P/E is only 4.4! The cheapest cement stock on the market.” You need to build sustainable profit and judge the price.
Last year’s numbers and today’s
Reported EPS: 1,500 rials
Of which: a land-sale gain of 300 rials and a currency translation gain of 100 rials per share (both one-off)
Today’s price: 6,600 rials
Usual payout ratio: 80%; expected sustainable nominal profit growth: 25% a year
Akhza return: 30%; risk premium: 5 to 10 percentage points
Expected return ≈ E/P × payout ratio + growth
What is sustainable EPS, without one-off items, in rials?
What is the P/E with sustainable EPS?
6,600 ÷ 1,100 = 6; not the 4.4 the channel said.
What is E/P with sustainable EPS, in percent? (one decimal place)
What is the expected return, in percent? (one decimal place)
Compare the 38.3% return with Akhza at 30% and a risk premium of 5 to 10 points.
It’s between 35 and 40%; slightly above the minimum, with a small margin of safety
It’s very cheap; it beats Akhza, and any return above Akhza is attractive
It’s below Akhza and has no appeal
The required level is 35 to 40%. The price is close to value, not an obvious opportunity.
What is the payback with EPS of 1,100 and 25% growth, in years? (one decimal place)
1,100 + 1,375 + 1,719 + 2,148 = 6,342 by year 4; the remaining 258 out of year five’s 2,686 ≈ 0.1, so about 4.1 years.
In 2 to 4 sentences, answer the channel’s author: why doesn’t a P/E of 4.4 show that Kuhsar Cement is cheap?

The EPS of 1,500 includes one-off items; with sustainable profit of 1,100 rials, the P/E is 6. The expected return is about 38%, which against Akhza at 30% plus a risk premium of 5 to 10 points is only slightly above the minimum. A payback of about 4 years is reasonable, but it isn’t obviously cheap.
With sustainable profit of 1,100 rials, the P/E is 6, not 4.4
A return of about 38% against Akhza + risk premium has a small margin
Payback of about 4 years; reasonable but not obviously cheap
Sustainable profit first, then any ratio.
Alborz Steel
Alborz Steel’s board has proposed a 100% capital increase from cash contributions. You’re a shareholder and must vote at the extraordinary meeting.
The capital-increase justification report
Current capital: 2,000 billion rials (2 billion shares)
Sustainable net profit: 600 billion rials (EPS 300 rials)
Share price: 2,000 rials (E/P 15%)
Proposal: a 100% increase from contributions (2,000 billion rials) for a rolling-mill project with forecast yearly profit of 200 billion rials
The profit structure and your portfolio
Sales 10,000, cost of sales 9,000, gross profit 1,000 billion rials (a 10% margin).
Your portfolio: 500 million tomans in 8 stocks; steel industry weight: 35%.
The adjusted price after a 100% increase from contributions? (P = 2,000, a = 1, b = 0)
What is the project’s return on the new money, in percent?
The project’s return is 10% and the current E/P 15%. The result for shareholders?
Dilutive; E/P on the adjusted price comes to about 13.3%
Value-creating; E/P after the project comes to about 17%
No effect; E/P stays at the same 15%
New profit of 800 billion on 4 billion shares = EPS 200; 200 ÷ 1,500 ≈ 13.3%, below the earlier 15%.
If the steel price falls 5% and cost of sales stays the same, by how many percent does gross profit fall?
Sales 9,500 − 9,000 = 500 against 1,000, that is half. A thin margin means high sensitivity.
In a 500-million-toman portfolio, what is a 15% cap per stock, in million tomans?
Steel’s weight in your portfolio is 35%. Following the portfolio rules, what do you do?
It’s above the industry cap (25 to 30%); I don’t add more, or I cut the weight
No problem; the weight cap is only for one stock, not for a whole industry in the portfolio
I raise the weight to 50% because steel is cheap
One government decision or world price can hit a whole industry.
Write your vote at Alborz Steel’s extraordinary meeting in 2 to 4 sentences, with a numerical reason.

I vote against. The project’s return is 10%, which is below the current E/P of 15% and the risk-free rate. After the capital increase, EPS falls to 200 rials and E/P on the adjusted price to about 13.3%; that is, dilution.
The project’s return (10%) is below the current E/P (15%)
It’s dilutive: EPS falls to 200 and E/P to about 13.3%
Conclusion: vote against, or demand a higher return for the project
New money only creates value when it earns more than the current situation.
Dasht Dairy

Dasht Dairy pays out most of its profit every year. You need to see whether it passes the Golden Three formula, what it means for a financial freedom plan, and work out a few FIS score variables from its latest reports.
5-year record (rials)
Average inflation over these years: about 35%. Operating profit positive in all 5 years; little bank debt.
Today’s price: 5,500 rials
5 (latest)
This year’s latest reports
EPS for the first 6 months of this year: 650 rials.
6-month sales: 4,800 billion rials; last year’s 6 months: 3,600 billion rials.
Trade receivables: 1,200 billion rials; total sales last year: 7,300 billion rials.
What is the payout ratio in the latest year, in percent?
What is the dividend yield at today’s price and the latest year’s DPS, in percent?
Compare year-on-year EPS growth with 35% inflation.
All 4 years were above 35% (about 37 to 40%)
Only the first year was above inflation (about 40%)
No year was above inflation (about 30%)
Does Dasht Dairy pass the Golden Three formula?
Yes; sustainable profit, a 90% payout and growth above inflation
No; the payout is low, below 60% of each year’s net profit
No; it has no sustainable profit and it swings
All three conditions hold in the numbers. Next step: also weigh the price, operating cash and price-control risk.
What is the theoretical price on the reopening day after the meeting, in rials? (price 5,500, DPS 990)
5,500 − 990 = 4,510; the money moves from one pocket to another.
With monthly costs of 45 million tomans and a dividend yield of 18%, how many million tomans of capital do you need for financial freedom?
45 × 12 ÷ 0.18 = 3,000 million tomans (3 billion).
What is the forward P/E by the FIS paper’s method (6-month profit × 2) at a price of 5,500 rials?
What is the cumulative 6-month sales growth, in percent?
How many days is the receivables collection period? (365-day year)
With the paper’s example (Akhza about 40%, a buy range of P/E 3.5 to 4), is a price of 5,500 rials in the buy range?
No; the forward P/E is about 4.2, and the buy ceiling at a P/E of 4 is a price of 5,200 rials
Yes; any P/E below 5 is in the buy range of the paper’s example, and 4.2 is below 5, so buying is right
Yes; because the company passes the Golden Three and the price doesn’t matter
Good quality isn’t enough; the price must also be in range. This is the paper’s example, not a fixed rule.
Write a short profile of Dasht Dairy in 2 to 4 sentences: the Golden Three, the dividend yield and one risk.

It passes the Golden Three: operating profit positive for 5 years, a 90% payout and EPS growth of about 38% against 35% inflation. The dividend yield at a price of 5,500 is about 18%. Risk: government price controls on dairy, or profit growth slowing below inflation.
All three conditions hold (sustainable profit, a 90% payout, growth above inflation)
A dividend yield of about 18%
One specific risk (e.g. price controls, growth below inflation, or payouts funded by loans)
This is analysis, not a buy recommendation.
Sepid Wind Power
Sepid Wind Power has a big project, and this year’s profit doesn’t represent the future, so a DCF is needed. The assumptions are on the table.
Assumptions (billion rials, in today’s prices)
Akhza 28% + equity risk premium 7 points → nominal rate 35%; expected long-term inflation 25%
Real free cash flow: year 1: 540, year 2: 570, year 3: 588, year 4: 600, and after that with 2% real growth
2 billion shares
What is the real discount rate, in percent?
The present value of year 1’s cash flow (540) at 8%?
The terminal value at the end of year 3 (with year 4’s flow and 2% growth)?
The present value of the first three years is 1,455 and the present value of the terminal value is 7,938. What share of the total is the terminal value, in percent? (one decimal place)
7,938 ÷ 9,393 ≈ 84.5%; within the usual 70 to 85% range, so always write it next to the result.
What is the value per share, in rials? (total value 9,393 billion rials, 2 billion shares; whole number)
An analyst discounted the nominal cash flow at the same 8% rate. The result?
The value comes out far higher than it really is; nominal and real don’t match
It’s correct; the 8% rate suits any flow, nominal or real makes no difference
The value comes out lower than it really is because the rate is low
Inflation is in the numerator but not in the denominator.
Why is P/B misleading for this power plant?
The assets are recorded at historical cost
Because the company has no profit and makes losses
Because P/B for a power plant is always zero
With inflation, book value is far below replacement value.
In 2 to 4 sentences, say how much you trust the DCF result for Sepid Power and why.

The value per share comes out at about 4,700 rials, but about 85% of it comes from the terminal value, so the result is very sensitive to the 8% rate and 2% growth. Sensitivity should be worked out with other rates and growth, and the result checked against peers’ multiples.
Most of the value (about 85%) comes from the terminal value
The result is sensitive to the discount rate and terminal growth; sensitivity analysis is needed
It should be compared with another method (peer multiples)
A DCF number with no sensitivity is a guess that looks precise.
Arya Parts
Arya Parts’ profit grew 25%, but something in the notes doesn’t look right. Fill in the profit-quality report card.
The last two years (billion rials)
Previous year
Latest year
Cash from operations (CFO)
Trade receivables
Bank loans
Notes and other numbers
Average total assets in the latest year: 5,000
NOPAT in the latest year: 900; capital employed: 6,000 (net fixed assets 3,000 + receivables 2,600 + inventory 1,400 − payables 1,000)
The depreciation method changed from declining-balance to straight-line in the latest year.
Main customer: a big carmaker that pays late.
Approved dividend: 10% of net profit.
Peers’ real WACC: about 8%.
What is the ratio of CFO to net profit in the latest year? (one decimal place)
200 ÷ 1,000 = 0.2; below 0.5 means a close look.
What is the accruals ratio in the latest year, in percent?
(1,000 − 200) ÷ 5,000 = 16%; most of the profit hasn’t turned into cash.
By how many percent did trade receivables grow? (one decimal place)
Which items are signs of earnings management?
Warning sign
Profit grew but operating cash fell
A change in the depreciation method in the latest year
A low payout alongside growing borrowing
Publishing reports on time
The auditor is the same as last year’s
The first three are among the seven signs of earnings management.
What is the ROIC in the latest year, in percent?
ROIC of 15% against a real WACC of 8%. The right reading?
ROIC is nominal and at historical cost; both must be made real before comparing
It definitely creates value because ROIC is nearly twice WACC and the gap is wide
It definitely destroys value because WACC is real
The denominator is at historical cost, and nominal ROIC in Iran is higher than the real figure.
Write Arya Parts’ profit-quality report card in 2 to 4 sentences.

Profit hasn’t turned into cash: CFO to profit is 0.2 and accruals are 16%. Receivables from the carmaker grew 73% and carry collection risk. The change in depreciation method and the low payout alongside more borrowing are signs of earnings management; I don’t believe the 25% profit growth.
Profit not turned into cash (CFO/NI 0.2, accruals 16%)
Receivables from the carmaker grew 73% (collection risk)
Signs of earnings management: the depreciation change, a low payout with borrowing
Read profit that doesn’t turn into cash with caution.
Sara in a Falling Market
The market has been falling for three months and Sara is tempted to sell everything. Read her notebook and help her write rules.
Sara’s notebook
“I bought Stock A 4 months ago at 10,000 rials; now it’s 6,000. I won’t sell until it gets back to my buying price.”
“Everyone in the Telegram group is selling; I should sell too.”
“I only read analyses that say Stock B will go up.”
“Last year I had 3 winning stocks; this time too I know which one will go up.”
Portfolio: 200 million tomans; Stock B: 80 million; she has taken 30 million of broker credit.
Link each sentence in Sara’s notebook to its bias.
I won’t sell until it gets back to my buying price
Loss aversion
Everyone’s selling, so am I
I only read the analyses that agree with me
This time too I know which one will go up
Antidotes: “If I didn’t own it today, would I buy it?”, the Codal file, writing the best opposing argument, and scoring your forecasts.
What percent of Sara’s portfolio is Stock B?
80 ÷ 200 = 40%; several times the 10 to 15% cap.
Stock A has fallen 40%. What percent rise is needed to get back to the buying price? (one decimal place)
10,000 ÷ 6,000 − 1 ≈ 66.7%; a big loss is hard to make up.
Which of Sara’s actions creates the biggest risk of ruin?
Broker credit (leverage)
Reading analyses
Keeping a trade journal
With leverage and daily price limits, she may get stuck in a sell queue and be forced to sell.
The right rule for Stock A after a 40% fall?
Check whether the reason for buying (sustainable profit) still holds; if it does, hold, otherwise sell
Wait until it gets back to the buying price, then decide; selling at a loss locks the loss in
Sell everything because the market is falling and the fall will continue
The buying price doesn’t matter to the market; the reason for buying does.
Write Sara a 2 to 4-sentence rule for the market’s next fall.

In a fall, I only check each stock’s reason for buying: if sustainable profit is still there I hold, and if not I sell, not because of my buying price or the Telegram group. No stock goes above 15% of the portfolio, and I don’t use leverage. I write every decision in my notebook before acting.
Decisions based on the reason for buying and sustainable profit, not the buying price or the crowd
A cap per stock (10 to 15%) and no leverage
Writing the decision in the notebook before acting
The antidote to fear isn’t recklessness; it’s a plan.
Kavir Minerals
9 months of the year have passed and you want to analyse Kavir Minerals in one go, from the monthly report to the decision.
Data
Cumulative 9-month sales this year: 18,000 billion rials; last year’s 9 months: 15,000; all of last year: 20,000 (the last quarter’s share is usually the same as last year’s)
Historical sustainable net profit margin: 20%; 4 billion shares
Price: 7,500 rials; Akhza 30%; payout ratio 70%; sustainable growth 20%
Disclosure quality: the last two monthly reports came out 12 days after the deadline, and the reason for the Aban correction wasn’t explained.
Estimated yearly sales, assuming the last quarter’s share is the same as last year’s?
Net profit at a 20% margin?
What is the estimated EPS, in rials?
4,800 billion ÷ 4 billion shares = 1,200
A 31.2% return against Akhza at 30% and the risk premium?
Below the required level (35 to 40%); not attractive at this price
Very attractive because it beats Akhza, and the risk premium doesn’t matter
It equals Akhza, so it’s risk-free and excellent
Only 1.2 points above Akhza; you aren’t paid for the equity risk.
What do the late monthly reports and the unexplained correction tell you?
Disclosure quality is poor; demand a higher company-specific risk premium
It doesn’t matter; only the final number counts
It means profit is higher than estimated and good news is on the way
A company that reports late and vaguely carries more uncertainty.
Put the 7 update steps for the next monthly report in order.
Compare with your own forecast
The rial effect on yearly profit
Writing in the notebook always comes before any action.
Write a 2 to 4-sentence decision note on Kavir Minerals for your notebook.

Estimated EPS is about 1,200 rials and the expected return about 31%, which is less than Akhza at 30% plus the risk premium; so I won’t buy at 7,500. Disclosure quality is also poor and calls for a bigger risk premium. I’ll check again with the next monthly report and the 7 steps.
EPS about 1,200 and an expected return of about 31%
Less than Akhza + risk premium; not at this price
Poor disclosure quality creates more risk
From the monthly report to the decision, all on one page.
Ofogh Holding
Ofogh Holding has traded below NAV for years, and one of its subsidiaries is in trouble. Weigh the value and the risk.
Portfolio and balance sheet (billion rials)
4 billion shares; price 2,100 rials. For simplicity, take the tax on a hypothetical sale as zero.
History: traded at a 30 to 40% discount to NAV for 5 years; dividend: 5% of net profit.
Subsidiary “Ofogh Construction”: capital 800, accumulated losses 500.
Market value of listed shares
Unlisted, at cost
Unlisted, estimated value
Cash and other assets
Liabilities
Total NAV with the unlisted holdings at estimated value?
What is NAV per share, in rials?
12,000 billion ÷ 4 billion shares = 3,000
The ratio of price to NAV (P/NAV)?
Is a 30% discount to NAV an opportunity?
Only with a trigger such as a high dividend; with 5 years of discount and a 5% payout it’s probably a trap
It’s definitely an opportunity; every discount closes eventually and patience is enough, even with no dividend
It means the company is bankrupt and should be avoided
A discount with no trigger can last for ever.
With capital of 800 and accumulated losses of 500, what applies to Ofogh Construction?
Article 141: accumulated losses above half the capital
No article; the losses are less than the capital
Only an auditor’s warning in the going-concern paragraph
500 is more than 400; an extraordinary meeting must decide on dissolving or continuing.
In NAV, we always count unlisted holdings at their book cost.
Historical cost is low under inflation; use a cautious estimated value and write down its assumption.
Write your view of Ofogh Holding in 2 to 4 sentences.

NAV per share is about 3,000 rials and the price 2,100, a 30% discount. But 5 years of discount and a payout of only 5% show there is no trigger for this value to reach shareholders. The subsidiary under Article 141 is also a risk; until I see a trigger, I don’t count the discount as an opportunity.
NAV per share about 3,000 and a 30% discount
A lasting discount and a low payout; a trigger is needed
The subsidiary under Article 141 is a risk
Until value reaches the shareholder, it exists only on paper.
